events/montanist-movement-156/summary: In Phrygia, Montanus and the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla delivered ecstatic oracles in the first person of the Paraclete, called for rigorous fasting and expected the New Jerusalem at Pepouza. Bishops in Asia condemned the movement, but it spread to Rome and North Africa, where Tertullian embraced it.
events/montanist-movement-156/causes/0: Desire for renewed prophecy and moral rigour
events/montanist-movement-156/causes/1: Strong apocalyptic hopes in Asia Minor
events/montanist-movement-156/consequenc: Church leaders sharpen the distinction between apostolic and ongoing prophecy
Influence on debates about the canon and church authority
events/diatessaron-170/title: Tatian's Diatessaron and early Syriac Christianity
events/diatessaron-170/summary: Tatian, a pupil of Justin, returned east and compiled the Diatessaron, a harmony of the four Gospels that became the standard Gospel text in Syriac-speaking churches until the fifth century. It reveals a vigorous Christianity in Mesopotamia with an ascetic bent.
events/diatessaron-170/causes/0: Spread of Christianity among Syriac speakers
events/diatessaron-170/consequences/1: Later replacement by the Peshitta separate Gospels
events/martyrs-of-lyon-177/summary: A mob-driven persecution killed some forty-eight Christians in Lyon, including the elderly bishop Pothinus and the slave girl Blandina, whose endurance was celebrated in a letter preserved by Eusebius. Irenaeus succeeded Pothinus as bishop.
events/martyrs-of-lyon-177/causes/0: Popular hostility and rumours of cannibalism and incest
events/martyrs-of-lyon-177/consequences/: Widely read martyr letter shaping Christian ideals
events/scillitan-martyrs-180/title: Scillitan martyrs: first dated Latin Christian text
events/scillitan-martyrs-180/summary: On 17 July 180 twelve Christians from Scillium in Numidia were beheaded at Carthage after refusing to swear by the emperor. The Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs, which mention 'the books and letters of Paul', are the earliest dated Christian document in Latin and the first evidence of African Christianity.
events/scillitan-martyrs-180/consequence: North Africa emerges as a heartland of Latin Christianity
events/irenaeus-against-heresies-180/sum: Irenaeus, a native of Asia Minor taught by Polycarp, refuted Valentinian and other Gnostic systems. He appealed to the rule of faith, the four Gospels and the succession of bishops, and taught that Christ 'recapitulated' humanity, undoing Adam's fall.
events/irenaeus-against-heresies-180/cau: Spread of Gnostic teachers in Gaul and Rome
events/irenaeus-against-heresies-180/con: Rule of faith and apostolic succession as tests of orthodoxy
events/catechetical-school-alexandria-18: Catechetical school of Alexandria under Pantaenus

Pantaenus, a converted Stoic, led the Christian school at Alexandria, followed by Clement and Origen. Eusebius reports that Pantaenus travelled to 'India' and found Christians there using a Gospel of Matthew in Hebrew letters — perhaps southern Arabia or India proper.
Alexandria's role as capital of Greek learning
Christian Platonism of Clement and Origen
events/quartodeciman-controversy-190/sum: Bishop Victor of Rome sought to excommunicate the churches of Asia, led by Polycrates of Ephesus, for keeping Easter on 14 Nisan rather than on Sunday. Irenaeus rebuked Victor for breaking communion over custom. The dispute foreshadowed later contests over Roman authority and the date of Easter.
events/quartodeciman-controversy-190/cau: Divergent Johannine and Roman paschal customs
events/quartodeciman-controversy-190/con: Sunday Easter becomes the norm; settled further at Nicaea
Precedent for debates over papal authority
events/edessa-church-flood-201/summary: The Chronicle of Edessa records that a flood in 201 damaged 'the temple of the church of the Christians' — one of the earliest references anywhere to a dedicated church building. Edessa, under its Abgarid kings, was by now a centre of Syriac-speaking Christianity; claims that Abgar VIII became Christian are debated.
events/edessa-church-flood-201/consequen: Edessa as the intellectual capital of Syriac Christianity
events/martyrdom-of-perpetua-203/summary: Vibia Perpetua, a young noblewoman and nursing mother, and the pregnant slave Felicity were killed in the amphitheatre at Carthage with other catechumens. Perpetua's prison diary, with her visions, is among the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman.
events/martyrdom-of-perpetua-203/consequ: Widely read in North African churches, even in liturgy
Ideals of martyr courage across class and gender
events/origen-moves-to-caesarea-231/summ: After a conflict with Bishop Demetrius of Alexandria, Origen moved to Caesarea in Palestine, where he taught, preached and built a great library. His Hexapla, commentaries and On First Principles made him the most prolific and influential theologian of the century, though some speculations were later condemned.
events/origen-moves-to-caesarea-231/caus: Dispute over Origen's ordination outside Alexandria
events/origen-moves-to-caesarea-231/cons: Caesarea library later used by Eusebius and Jerome
events/dura-europos-house-church-232/sum: At the frontier city of Dura-Europos on the Euphrates, a private house was converted into a church around 232–240, with an assembly room and a baptistery painted with the Good Shepherd, Adam and Eve and the women at the tomb. Buried when the Persians besieged the city in 256, it is the oldest securely identified church building.
events/dura-europos-house-church-232/cau: Growth of congregations in the eastern frontier
events/dura-europos-house-church-232/con: Key evidence for early Christian art and baptism
events/decian-persecution-250/summary: Emperor Decius ordered all inhabitants to sacrifice to the gods and obtain a certificate (libellus). It was the first empire-wide persecution; Bishop Fabian of Rome died, Origen was tortured, and many Christians lapsed. The question of how to readmit the lapsed divided the churches.
events/decian-persecution-250/causes/0: Decius' programme to restore traditional religion amid crisis
events/decian-persecution-250/consequenc: Cyprian's theology of the church's unity
events/novatianist-schism-251/summary: When Cornelius was elected bishop of Rome and favoured readmitting penitent lapsed Christians, the rigorist presbyter Novatian was consecrated as rival bishop. His 'church of the pure' survived for centuries; Cyprian of Carthage sided with Cornelius.
events/novatianist-schism-251/causes/0: Dispute over the lapsed after Decius
events/novatianist-schism-251/consequenc: Rigorist churches lasting into the 5th century
events/rebaptism-controversy-256/summary: African synods under Cyprian held that baptism outside the church was invalid and converts from schism must be baptized; Stephen of Rome insisted that such baptism be recognised by laying on of hands. The dispute, cut short by persecution, foreshadowed the Donatist conflict.
events/rebaptism-controversy-256/causes/: Converts from Novatianist and other groups
events/rebaptism-controversy-256/consequ: Augustine later develops the theory of valid but fruitless sacraments
events/valerian-persecution-258/title: Valerian persecution and death of Cyprian
events/valerian-persecution-258/summary: Valerian's edicts targeted clergy and confiscated church property. Sixtus II of Rome was beheaded with his deacons and Cyprian of Carthage was executed on 14 September 258. Gallienus ended the persecution in 260, beginning forty years of relative peace.
events/valerian-persecution-258/causes/0: Imperial crisis and search for scapegoats
events/valerian-persecution-258/conseque: Forty years' peace allowing growth and church building
events/shapur-deportations-260/title: Shapur I deports Roman Christians to Persia
events/shapur-deportations-260/summary: After capturing Antioch and the emperor Valerian, the Sasanian king Shapur I resettled thousands of Roman captives, many of them Christians, in Persian cities such as Gundeshapur. These communities, alongside native Syriac converts, strengthened the church that became the Church of the East.
events/shapur-deportations-260/consequen: Greek- and Syriac-speaking congregations in Persia
Later Persian suspicion of Christians as a Roman fifth column
events/paul-of-samosata-deposed-268/titl: Synod of Antioch deposes Paul of Samosata
events/paul-of-samosata-deposed-268/summ: A synod at Antioch deposed its bishop Paul of Samosata for teaching that Jesus was a man indwelt by the divine Word rather than the Word incarnate. The synod rejected the term homoousios in Paul's sense — a fact later cited against Nicaea.
events/paul-of-samosata-deposed-268/cons: Precedent for synodal deposition of bishops
Complicated the later reception of homoousios
events/antony-goes-to-desert-270/title: Antony withdraws to the Egyptian desert
events/antony-goes-to-desert-270/place/n: Monastery of St Antony, Eastern Desert
events/antony-goes-to-desert-270/summary: Hearing the Gospel call to sell all, the Coptic peasant Antony gave away his property and withdrew progressively deeper into the desert, eventually to the Red Sea mountains. Athanasius' Life of Antony made him the model of the hermit and launched monasticism across the Christian world.
events/antony-goes-to-desert-270/causes/: Decline of martyrdom as the path of heroic witness
events/antony-goes-to-desert-270/consequ: Life of Antony shapes Augustine's conversion and Western monasticism
events/conversion-of-armenia-301/summary: According to Armenian tradition, Gregory the Illuminator, after years in a pit at Khor Virap, healed King Tiridates III, who made Christianity the religion of the kingdom — traditionally dated 301, though many scholars prefer c. 314. Armenia thus claims to be the first Christian state, with Etchmiadzin as its mother cathedral.
events/conversion-of-armenia-301/causes/: Missionary work of Gregory, trained in Cappadocian Caesarea
Armenian desire to distinguish itself from Persia
events/conversion-of-armenia-301/consequ: Armenian Apostolic Church and later Armenian alphabet and literature
events/diocletian-persecution-303/summar: Beginning on 23 February 303 at Nicomedia, Diocletian and Galerius ordered churches destroyed, Scriptures surrendered and eventually universal sacrifice. The persecution was harshest in Egypt and the East, lasting until Galerius' edict of toleration in 311 (and later under Maximinus Daia).
events/diocletian-persecution-303/conseq: Thousands of martyrs, especially in Egypt (the Coptic 'Era of Martyrs' calendar dates from 284)
Failure of persecution paves way for Constantine
events/donatist-schism-311/summary: Many Numidian bishops rejected Caecilian as bishop of Carthage because one of his consecrators was alleged to be a traditor who had handed over Scriptures in the persecution. They elected Majorinus, then Donatus, creating a rival church of the martyrs that dominated parts of Africa for a century.
events/donatist-schism-311/causes/1: Cyprianic theology of a pure church
events/donatist-schism-311/consequences/: Augustine's theology of church and sacraments
events/edict-of-milan-313/summary: Meeting at Milan, Constantine and Licinius agreed to grant Christians and all others freedom of worship and to restore confiscated church property. Following Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge (312) under the sign of Christ, it began the transformation of Christianity into the favoured religion of the empire.
events/edict-of-milan-313/consequences/0: Imperial patronage, basilica building and clerical privileges
events/pachomius-koinonia-320/summary: Pachomius, a former soldier, organised monks in the Thebaid into a koinonia of monasteries with a written rule, shared labour and obedience to an abbot. By his death in 346 thousands followed his system, the model for cenobitic monasticism East and West.
events/pachomius-koinonia-320/consequenc: Cenobitic rule, later influential on Basil and Benedict
events/council-of-nicaea-325/summary: Convened by Constantine, some 250–300 bishops condemned Arius' teaching that the Son was a creature and declared the Son 'of one substance' (homoousios) with the Father. The council also set the date of Easter and issued canons on church order, including the precedence of Alexandria, Rome and Antioch.
events/council-of-nicaea-325/longText: The crisis began in Alexandria around 318 when the presbyter Arius taught that the Son of God, though first and highest of creatures, 'was not before he was begotten' — there was when he was not. Bishop Alexander, with his deacon Athanasius, saw this as undermining salvation itself: only one who is truly God can unite humanity to God. Constantine, newly sole ruler and eager for unity, summoned bishops mostly from the East to the lakeside town of Nicaea in May–June 325. The creed they adopted, built on an existing baptismal creed, added anti-Arian phrases — 'from the substance of the Father', 'true God from true God', 'begotten not made', 'homoousios' — with anathemas. Arius and two bishops refused to sign and were exiled. Nicaea did not end the controversy: homoousios was suspect to many as unscriptural or Sabellian, and for half a century imperial policy swung toward Homoian compromises until Constantinople (381). Nevertheless, Nicaea became the template for ecumenical councils and its creed (as expanded in 381) is confessed by Catholic, Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, Church of the East and most Protestant churches. Nontrinitarian groups regard it as a departure from apostolic teaching under imperial pressure; its defenders reply that it articulated the faith already present in Scripture and worship.
events/council-of-nicaea-325/consequence: Model of imperially summoned ecumenical council
